channel.title: Forbes Technology Council
channel.description: Technology leadership and innovation insights from Forbes Technology Council

item.title: 19 Startup Habits Tech Companies Should Never Outgrow
item.description: Forbes Technology Council members name startup habits that established tech companies should keep as process and hierarchy pile up. Vytautas Savickas of Oxylabs urges firms to keep turning down business that doesn't fit, Rob Sloan of Zscaler wants authority pushed to "the people closest to the problem" and Akhilesh Sharma of A3Logics argues every new priority should displace an old one. Sergii Grushai of Peeklogic recommends running a process by hand before automating it, noting that "roughly a third of flows" in the mature organizations Peeklogic audits either duplicate another or barely run.
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: Closing The Enterprise AI Security Gap: From Blind Spots To Stronger Defenses
item.description: Mudavatu uses EchoLeak, a since-patched Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw disclosed in June 2025 that let a crafted email trigger data exfiltration without a click, to argue that enterprise AI security now depends on "enforceable boundaries" more than on reassuring model behavior. The proposed framework assesses six blind spots, including unverified model artifacts, agents whose credentials outlive being disabled, data leaking through tool calls and logs, and trust inherited between agents, then phases in controls starting with agent discovery, outbound monitoring and kill switches. Mudavatu would count a control as closed only with evidence that it works, and offers a simple test: disable an agent and confirm its downstream actions actually stop.
item.dc:creator: Vasanth Mudavatu

item.title: Why The Same Threat Means Different Things To Different Companies
item.description: Goel, CEO of Cyware, argues that threat intelligence feeds know the threat but nothing about a subscriber's own assets, identities and controls, so relevance has to be produced by measuring each indicator against a specific environment. The same indicator can call for immediate isolation at a company where it maps to a critical internet-facing application and mere logging where it touches a decommissioned service; without that context, Goel writes, an indicator "is just a rumor about someone else's network." That matters more as platforms and AI agents rather than human analysts consume intelligence to prioritize and act, since raw one-size-fits-all feeds leave them unable to tell a live risk from an irrelevant one.
item.dc:creator: Anuj Goel

item.title: The AI Control Gap: Companies Adopting AI Must Learn What Wall Street Learned The Hard Way
item.description: Kaluvuri, CEO of ApyHub, points to a large bank that gives an AI agent a name, a login ID and a manager, and argues that approval workflows can't oversee software taking thousands of autonomous actions because "the risk lives in the path." Finance learned this through episodes like Knight Capital's loss of more than $460 million in 45 minutes in 2012 and moved controls into the execution path, with the SEC's market access rule requiring them to stay under a firm's "direct and exclusive control." Kaluvuri urges buyers of agent platforms to ask where runtime controls are enforced and who can change them, and in some cases to keep a workflow under human supervision until adequate controls exist.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Kaluvuri

item.title: Stop Measuring Technology Adoption And Start Measuring What It Changes
item.description: Kolandaisami, a doctoral researcher, recounts an organization that bought an AI coding assistant without studying where it would help and then set a KPI that developers met simply by showing they had adopted the tool. Citing one 2025 study that estimated a 26.08% gain in completed tasks and another that found experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with the AI tools tested, Kolandaisami argues that results vary by environment and that metrics should come from the problem, such as the full cycle from requirements to release rather than programming time alone. Low usage should first be treated as information rather than a performance problem, and pilots should test whether a tool fits a team's people and processes, because "Technology needs to work for us."
item.dc:creator: Gayathri Kolandaisami

item.title: Your AI Governance Stops At The Screen: The Blind Spot In AI-Driven Document Workflows
item.description: Ercanbrack, CTO at Vasion, argues that AI governance is usually scoped to the application while documents keep moving through printing, faxing, exporting and scanning, a gap long covered by employees who could remember what they produced. Agents remove that undocumented human control just as adoption accelerates: Deloitte's 2026 survey found nearly three in four companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, while one in five reports a mature governance model for autonomous agents. Ercanbrack suggests following one operational document from creation to disposition and testing identity, authorization, audit and retention at each handoff, since "The handoffs are where governance stops without announcing it."
item.dc:creator: Corey Ercanbrack

item.title: The Industrial Revolution Of Intelligence: AI Energy Infrastructure
item.description: Wong, an AI research fellow at Info-Tech Research Group, sorts national AI energy strategies into four types: sovereign regulation-driven (Canada, Australia, the EU), market-driven (the U.S. and UK), localization-driven (Japan, and South Korea, which is directing 18.4 GW of data center workloads out of Seoul) and state-driven China. Wong proposes judging a strategy along its energy value chain, from power sourcing and grid management, where AI racks demanding 130 to 600 kW push operators toward ±400V or 800V DC systems, to thermal management, where some cold-climate operators sell 60- to 80-degree Celsius waste heat to district heating networks. Builders should also be ready to answer community backlash over data centers with a focus on sustainability, environmental impact and accountability.
item.dc:creator: Bill Wong

item.title: If Your AI Isn't Working, Fix The Foundation
item.description: Bise, CTO of Inbenta, says the knowledge underneath a customer-experience AI deployment, not the model, explains nearly every underperforming one Bise has examined, so buying a new platform is often "an expensive way to rebuild the same problem." Before another vendor evaluation, Bise suggests checking whether content is structured for a model to parse, counting duplicate knowledge stores left from older intent-matching systems or split by channel, and confirming that subject matter experts can fix wrong answers without filing an engineering ticket. AI can now structure and tag content in weeks rather than quarters, and fixing the knowledge layer costs a fraction of a six-figure platform replacement while producing an audit trail regulators can follow.
item.dc:creator: Merlin Bise

item.title: Identity Governance And The Challenge Of AI Agents Moving At Machine Speed
item.description: Garg, CEO of One Identity, argues that companies don't need new governance architectures for AI agents, because existing identity governance and administration (IGA) and privileged access management (PAM) tools can ask machines the same questions asked of humans. An agent acting for a user should get at most that user's permissions, and each autonomous service needs its own identity, supervisor and role-specific permissions so its actions can be traced and its access revoked at machine speed. Citing Microsoft's deprecation of code access security and the early internet's turn to signatures and certificates, Garg writes that an agent's ability to reason about an action doesn't grant authority to take it, a decision that "must remain external to the model" and be enforced through identity infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Praerit Garg

item.title: AI Voice Agents Are Easy To Demo; Production Is Where The Engineering Begins
item.description: Picolini, a technology executive whose company builds contact-center platforms, says voice AI demos are easy, but real calls bring degraded carrier audio, speakerphone background noise and brief acknowledgments, where a simple "okay" can stop an agent mid-explanation. Picolini recommends testing over actual phone routes, caching likely-needed customer data (some deployments use Redis) to avoid multi-second API waits, verifying identity rather than trusting a recognized number, and defining human-transfer triggers that pass along a concise summary. Some audio delays over SIP appeared only at thousands of concurrent calls, and as Picolini puts it, "A good demo proves the AI can talk."
item.dc:creator: Alexandro Picolini

item.title: Tokens Built The Digital AI Business. Physical AI Needs A Different Unit
item.description: Barbello, co-founder and COO of Archetype AI, argues that per-token billing borrowed from language models fits poorly with industrial AI, where cameras and vibration sensors stream data around the clock and that data is often too proprietary to leave the facility. One Archetype municipal customer's intersection cameras each produce about 43 gigabytes a day, an estimated $850,000 to $1 million a year just to move to the cloud, so a distilled model runs on hardware the city already owns. Barbello's alternative is "Price the asset, not the traffic": licensing per machine, facility or application so finance teams know what scaling from 10 machines to 1,000 will cost, though that can be less economical for equipment analyzed only occasionally.
item.dc:creator: Brandon Barbello

item.title: Open-Source Dependencies: 19 Trust Signals Worth Checking
item.description: Forbes Technology Council members list signals beyond popularity and download counts for judging open-source dependencies, including the size of a package's transitive dependency graph, verifiable provenance, reproducible builds and OpenSSF Scorecard results. Persistent Systems' Mukul Arora says to check when maintainers last responded to a vulnerability report rather than when they last pushed code, calling a heavily starred repository with an 18-month-old unresolved security issue "a liability with good documentation." Other panelists flag newer risks: Guickly's Prashant Jalan warns that more dependencies now arrive because an AI model suggested them, and Atlas Cloud's Jerry Tang notes that open-weight model licenses can restrict commercial use even when the surrounding code carries an MIT license.
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: Your Monitoring Stack Isn’t The Problem. The Detection-To-Ownership Gap Is
item.description: Sharon, founder and CEO of OnPage, argues that a monitoring stack can catch a failure quickly and the response still stall, because emails, shared inboxes and Slack or Teams posts confirm only that an alert arrived, not that a qualified responder took charge. Since "Delivery is not ownership", Sharon proposes tracking detection-to-ownership time, breaking it into delivery, acknowledgment and confirmed ownership, and testing the workflow during shift changes, after hours and when the primary responder is unavailable. The fixes include stricter paging criteria so routine warnings land in dashboards or tickets, plus schedule-based routing that escalates automatically when no one acknowledges a critical page.
item.dc:creator: Judit Sharon

item.title: From Pilots To Payoff: The Top IT Priorities Every Executive Should Accomplish Before Year-End
item.description: Francis, a technology evangelist at PFU America and Ricoh Document Scanners, urges executives to use the rest of 2026, with 2027 budgets already in planning, to check whether AI is delivering returns, proving value in one workflow with quarter-over-quarter KPIs before expanding. Vendor risk belongs on the list too: Francis points to Anthropic's suspension of global access to Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 after a U.S. export control directive as a reason to identify fallback models now, alongside Gartner's projection that more than a third of enterprises will run localized AI platforms by 2027. Francis also stresses fixing bad data, which 43% of surveyed data and analytics leaders called the biggest barrier, and preparing employees so that consequential decisions stay with people rather than AI.
item.dc:creator: Scott Francis

item.title: AI's Workforce Gap And The Lessons We Keep Forgetting
item.description: Marangella, chief marketing and product officer at EdgeConneX, argues the AI build-out is limited as much by skilled labor as by chips and power, citing a construction shortage of roughly 439,000 workers and McKinsey's estimate that the U.S. will need 130,000 more electricians by 2030. Pointing to the World War II Training Within Industry program and Northern Virginia Community College's accredited data center operations degree, Marangella says workforce gaps close when training is treated as critical infrastructure. Local resistance is real, with Gallup finding seven in 10 Americans opposed to an AI data center nearby, and Marangella contends communities accept infrastructure once it is "built with them" through transparency, local hiring and promises that are kept.
item.dc:creator: Phillip Marangella

item.title: AI Slop Is Turning Bug Bounty Programs Into A Security Liability
item.description: Geffen, CEO and co-founder of Novee Security, warns that AI-generated bug bounty reports now look detailed and plausible even when wrong, so analysts spend hours disproving findings that took minutes to file, and HackerOne reported a more than 100% jump in report volume after new AI models arrived in February. The curl project ended its monetary bounty in January 2026 after its share of confirmed vulnerabilities fell below 5%, and later stopped taking reports for all of July even after quality recovered. Geffen writes that "Triage latency is just dwell time you've handed to an adversary", and argues programs should demand reproducibility, demonstrated impact and context, and reward proven exploitability and verified fixes over volume.
item.dc:creator: Ido Geffen

item.title: Data Sovereignty Isn't About Where Your Data Lives—It's About Who's In Control
item.description: McGrattan, chief technology officer at Actian, argues that data residency is not the same as sovereignty, pointing to a June 2025 French Senate hearing where a Microsoft executive said he could not guarantee that Azure data stored in France would never be handed to U.S. authorities without consent. Calling sovereignty "an architectural property rather than a compliance initiative", McGrattan recommends mapping critical data, external dependencies and alternatives for each critical service, with the tightest control reserved for identity systems, customer data and intellectual property. AI agents raise the stakes because organizations must explain which data informed a decision, yet in a 2026 BARC survey 89% called sovereignty important while just 10% had budget for it.
item.dc:creator: Emma McGrattan

item.title: The Evaluation Framework: The Most Underbuilt Part Of An AI System
item.description: Dhaduk, CTO and co-founder of Simform, describes assessing a production AI system that had regressed while its team had no way to compare the last-known-good version with a proposed fix, because the measurement infrastructure had never been built. Dhaduk argues evaluation should act as a release gate, built on a maintained set of representative examples that grows with each meaningful production failure, consistent scoring and thresholds set in advance for regressions serious enough to block a change. CTOs often defer that work for more visible features, but the cost returns as manual revalidation on every release, and Dhaduk judges changes by the "fully loaded cost per resolved outcome" rather than inference spend alone.
item.dc:creator: Hiren Dhaduk

item.title: AI Is The Accommodation Nobody Has To Approve
item.description: Goyal, CEO of Think AI, who had polio and has dyslexia, writes that founders with disabilities have no HR department to grant accommodations, so AI becomes "the accommodation you can give yourself." Citing AEO data, Goyal notes these entrepreneurs average about $61,000 in revenue against $135,000 for others yet use generative AI at more than twice the rate, and describes a 3,200-mile road trip made possible by supervised self-driving and an AI trip planner. Goyal's own setup includes an automated process that shrank podcast preparation from 24 to 30 hours to two or three, bookkeeping from a read-only copy of accounting data, and an "AI C-suite" of agents on an isolated computer barred from deleting anything or contacting clients.
item.dc:creator: Devendra Goyal

item.title: How Modular Data Centers Will Scale AI Infrastructure
item.description: Altizer, president and CEO of Compu Dynamics, argues that AI racks drawing 150 to 250 kilowatts leave cloud-era data halls as mostly empty space, and predicts campuses that standardize power, liquid cooling and networking while factory-built white-space modules plug in and get swapped as GPUs advance. Modules can also drop traditional UPS systems and diesel generators from the start and cut an 18-to-24-month build to six to nine months, Altizer says, likening production to automotive assembly lines. Buyers should check whether a modular partner truly manufactures at scale and can deliver a turnkey solution, since the aim is "token factories rather than architectural trophies."
item.dc:creator: Steve Altizer

item.title: Management Mistakes That Throttle Innovation On Tech Teams
item.description: Forbes Technology Council members identify management habits that quietly discourage experimentation, from punishing well-designed experiments that fail to stacking approval layers and demanding projected ROI on a two-week test. Amazon's Swapnil Upganlawar recommends separating learning goals from ship dates, noting that only 13% of AI users in Microsoft's 2026 survey said reinvention was rewarded when results fell short, while WitnessAI's Rick Caccia warns that blanket AI tool bans simply push employees onto personal devices and accounts. Other panelists propose keeping some sprint capacity unplanned or giving teams a small preapproved budget and time box, with a business case requested only after a test produces evidence.
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: The Future Of AI Will Be Decided In The Physical World
item.description: Matlantis CEO and Preferred Networks co-founder Daisuke Okanohara argues that AI's progress over the next decade will be limited less by intelligence than by physics: by some engineering estimates, moving data between memory and processor uses ten to a hundred times more energy than the computation itself, and nearly every hardware advance depends on slow materials discovery. Rather than spending through those walls with more chips and data centers, Okanohara urges designing materials, devices, chips and systems together and using AI simulation to screen materials early, noting that Matlantis has seen work that once demanded roughly 20 years of conventional calculation finish in about a week. Leaders should build in-house teams that can read AI results critically, Okanohara writes, and "Reserve for humans every decision that cannot be undone", such as committing capital.
item.dc:creator: Daisuke Okanohara

item.title: Why Individual AI Gains Don’t Add Up To Company Value
item.description: Orient Software CTO Son Nguyen argues that AI is making individual employees faster without making companies smarter, pointing to McKinsey's finding that 89% of organizations use AI but only 37% attribute at least some EBIT impact to it, a share unchanged from the prior year. Nguyen traces the gap to scattered knowledge, inconsistent definitions across departments, answers without sources and corrections that never leave a single conversation, and proposes a "company brain" built as an operating model rather than bought as a product. Such a system should pass five tests (evidence, shared meaning, permissions, learning and executive ownership), and Nguyen suggests starting by measuring the "time to trusted answers" for questions teams ask every week.
item.dc:creator: Son Nguyen

item.title: Houston, We Have A Communications Problem: Why Silence After A Breach Is Killing Trust
item.description: CoinRoutes co-founder and CEO Ian Weisberger argues that with cyberattacks on financial firms arriving near-weekly and AI making them easier, the bigger failure is silence afterward, contrasting Revolut and Bitget, which acknowledged their incidents and explained their response, with a portfolio management provider whose attack left CoinRoutes unable to answer shared clients' questions about possibly exposed trading data. Weisberger notes that CoinRoutes is contractually committed to post-mortems within 24 to 48 hours, even for five-minute outages, and calls on firms to acknowledge breaches within hours and keep partners updated until the picture is complete. Before anything goes wrong, Weisberger suggests asking providers when they will first make contact, what a stolen key or login would let an attacker do and whether one compromised account can reach other clients.
item.dc:creator: Ian Weisberger

item.title: Trusted AI Governance Starts Where Intent Becomes Action
item.description: WSO2 CTO Asanka Abeysinghe argues that because AI agents now call tools, invoke APIs and delegate work, governance must move beyond reviewing model outputs to the boundary "where intent becomes action", checking whether each action had the right authority, context and purpose. Abeysinghe says trust comes from architecture that makes agents inspectable, attributable and bounded, which requires pairing inline controls built into each agent with infrastructure-enforced controls at gateways and other shared enforcement points. Leaders are urged to start by discovering agents they can't yet see, give agents their own identities instead of shared service accounts and capture evidence after actions, since "Without evidence, governance becomes a claim."
item.dc:creator: Asanka Abeysinghe

item.title: Don't Surrender Standards: Who Decides Whether AI Work Is Any Good?
item.description: Quickbase Chief Product Officer Marcus Torres warns that as AI takes over drafting, coding and analysis, workers slide from creators to approvers and risk losing the judgment that hands-on work once built, noting that developer surveys show trust in AI-generated work falling even as usage climbs. Torres argues that IT, built to judge safety, governance and risk, can't decide whether a message persuades or an analysis answers the right question, so each team should own its own definition of quality, supported by governed environments with clear guardrails. Whether AI can build is settled, Torres writes, and the harder question is "Who decides if the work is any good?"
item.dc:creator: Marcus Torres

item.title: The Future Of AI Security Is Better Judgment, Not More Automation
item.description: Databricks CISO Omar Khawaja writes that the Databricks AI Security Framework catalogs 97 risks across 13 components of an AI system, but argues that context rather than a checklist determines which matter, since the same capability can be low-risk in one deployment and serious in another. Khawaja's team screens systems with a "lethal trifecta" of questions (does the AI touch sensitive data, is it exposed to untrusted content, can it change another system's state) and applies heightened controls when all three overlap, as with an agent that reads social media alongside customer data and writes back to internal systems. With exploit times down to days and Gartner predicting Fortune 500 companies will run more than 150,000 AI agents within two years, Khawaja recommends widening agents' permissions gradually and keeping human judgment where it matters most.
item.dc:creator: Omar Khawaja

item.title: From Cameo To Lead Role: AI Takes Over Ransomware
item.description: Cato Networks threat intelligence VP Etay Maor argues that AI has "democratized the ransomware attack vector", letting inexperienced affiliates handle the network mapping, target selection and negotiation that once took skilled operators days or weeks. Maor cites a group that handed negotiations to an AI chatbot that pressured victims around the clock, attackers who used a widely available AI coding tool to break into at least six organizations, and newer kits whose sellers claim an LLM runs the control panel, alongside IBM's count of a 49% rise in active ransomware groups and RaaS services selling for as little as $40 a month. Defenders, Maor writes, should watch for telltale signs such as heavily commented AI-written scripts or servers suddenly contacting AI services, and should keep unchangeable offline backups and test restores regularly.
item.dc:creator: Etay Maor

item.title: When AI Gets It Wrong: Why Exception Handling Is The New Finance Discipline
item.description: Trintech CTO Sunil Padiyar warns that as AI agents move from summarizing to classifying transactions and resolving exceptions in finance, a wrong decision can become part of the financial process before anyone reviews it and repeat across hundreds or thousands of transactions, so accuracy alone is an incomplete measure. Padiyar calls for exception handling that shows reviewers what an agent considered and concluded, sets thresholds for when humans take over and treats recurring exceptions as data in a cycle of "detect, explain, contain, resolve and learn." Beyond automation rates, leaders should ask how quickly an error was detected and contained and design for failure from the start, because the real test is "whether finance remains in control when it gets the answer wrong."
item.dc:creator: Sunil Padiyar

item.title: The Entrepreneurial Executive: How To Lead With Resiliency And Stamina
item.description: SmartSense president Guy Yehiav argues that volatile markets and compressed innovation cycles call for executives with entrepreneurial resiliency and stamina, qualities that emerge once founders take on investment, personal resources and responsibility for the financial stability of employees' families. Large companies struggle to replicate that, Yehiav writes, because small innovation teams stay accountable to quarterly targets and other competing priorities, and speculative breakthrough projects lack the urgency of modernizing an existing product. The proposed remedy is a startup-like company within a company, with dedicated teams insulated from operational demands, incentives tied to the initiative's own success, milestone-based funding and outcome-based metrics in place of traditional KPIs.
item.dc:creator: Guy Yehiav

item.title: To Defend Against AI Attackers, Start Thinking Like One
item.description: Surf AI CEO Yair Grindlinger argues that AI makes attackers faster, more persistent and broader in skill, able to chain several low- or medium-risk weaknesses into a critical attack path, citing CrowdStrike's finding that average criminal breakout time fell to 29 minutes and Hugging Face's account of an autonomous agent that took roughly 17,600 actions, most of them failed, while breaching part of its infrastructure. Grindlinger writes that defenders split into cloud, identity and IT teams miss connections attackers see, so prioritization should weigh exposure and attack chains rather than severity alone, even as many organizations still can't close basic critical exposures because asset ownership records are out of date. The prescription is to know every asset and its owner, run continuous automation on that knowledge and assign someone to think about exposure holistically, because "defenders cannot depend entirely on human-speed processes."
item.dc:creator: Yair Grindlinger

item.title: The ERP Migration Blind Spots That Technology Alone Can't Fix
item.description: APGAR North America CEO Bruno Billy writes that ERP migrations often stumble because teams begin configuring before agreeing on basic business definitions, such as whether a customer is the distributor that pays the invoice or the business that uses the product, and those conflicts can surface late in integration testing or financial reconciliation. Billy recommends defining entities, relationships and hierarchies up front, testing that model against real legacy records, and separating what must be written in ink across the enterprise from what can be written in pencil for local needs. Authority over master data should be assigned at the attribute or process level and sustained after go-live, because an ERP "encodes a model of your business."
item.dc:creator: Bruno Billy

item.title: AI Pods Are Redefining The Unit Of Software Delivery
item.description: Instinctools CEO Alexey Spas argues that coding agents are shifting software delivery from adding headcount to the AI pod, a compact, senior-led team accountable for a defined outcome, with agents supporting work from requirements drafting to testing while humans own business context, quality and security. In-house pods stay close to the product and keep their lessons inside the company but take time to mature and struggle to cover brief needs such as security or UX expertise, while external pods bring patterns tested across projects but lack institutional knowledge. Spas suggests a hybrid "borrow, prove, then build" approach that uses an outsourced pod as a prototype for a team built later, and says the operating model doesn't have to be permanent.
item.dc:creator: Alexey Spas

item.title: AI Is Making The App Optional
item.description: Pally co-founder Haz Hubble writes that when the AI messaging assistant ran as its own app, fewer than 20% of new users were still active in their second month, but after it moved into iMessage, where users sign up by texting a number, month-two retention rose above 70%. Hubble compares that approach with new hardware such as OpenAI's planned Jony Ive device and WeChat-style super-apps, argues messaging is the only path that asks for no new habit, and cites Satya Nadella's prediction that "The notion that business applications exist will probably collapse." Platform risk remains, as WhatsApp's January 2026 ban on general-purpose AI assistants on its business platform showed, so Hubble advises keeping logic on one's own infrastructure and predicts most consumer apps will work mainly as back-ends within five years.
item.dc:creator: Haz Hubble

item.title: How CISOs Can Set Guardrails On AI Agents Without Killing Adoption
item.description: CloudEagle.ai CEO Nidhi Jain points to a U.K. AI Security Institute disclosure of an agent under evaluation that created fake identities to try to socially engineer an open-source maintainer, and to Cloud Security Alliance findings that 65% of enterprises have had an AI agent-related security incident and 82% have unknown agents running. Because agents inherit their deployers' permissions, hold OAuth tokens across connected systems and outlive their use cases, Jain recommends scoped identities, human approval for high-risk actions such as moving money or changing production configurations, action-level audit logs and an expiration date for every agent. For agents already live, Jain advises inventorying every platform, cross-checking OAuth grants and retiring orphaned agents, under the principle that "Friction scales with risk," so read-only agents can keep full speed.
item.dc:creator: Nidhi Jain

item.title: The Case For Pre-Breach Intelligence: Why Buying Access Before Attackers Do Beats Cleaning Up
item.description: Austin Berglas of Nardello & Co., a former head of FBI New York Cyber, argues that security budgets favor post-breach response even though IBM puts the average breach at $4.44 million and 241 days to identify and contain. Most intrusions start with initial access brokers selling footholds on criminal forums, where Rapid7 researchers found the average base price "rose from $2,726 in 2024 to $113,275 in the second half of 2025," and KELA found access often sells within one to three days of listing. Pre-breach intelligence, which monitors and sometimes legally buys access in those markets, gives organizations time to rotate credentials and patch the route before an attack, including for compromised vendors, and Berglas urges leaders to ask whether access to their network is for sale today.
item.dc:creator: Austin Berglas

item.title: Meeting AI Demand Starts With The Right Infrastructure
item.description: CoreSite CEO Juan Font compares enterprises' rush to consume AI tokens to the early cloud era's loosely overseen spending, arguing the bigger problem is often the infrastructure behind deployments, where GPUs are scarce and long-haul fiber can leave costly chips waiting for data. Font says colocation data centers near population centers and network hubs can act as inferencing hubs with direct connections between private and public infrastructure, and that agentic workloads such as Meta's Muse assistant will need inexpensive, high-speed links to models. The heaviest demand for that interconnection capacity comes from AI companies such as Anthropic, OpenAI and CoreWeave, and Font says it already outpaces supply, making colocation "a matter of survival."
item.dc:creator: Juan Font

item.title: Why Good Product Management Starts On The Factory Floor
item.description: Ultimo chief product officer Harmjan Derksen argues that enterprise software teams should spend more time observing end users than reading analyst reports, recalling a plant team lead who spent 45 minutes every morning cross-referencing breakdown reports and shift logs. Shadowing maintenance crews taught Derksen to treat workarounds such as a paper notebook beside a tablet as product feedback and to test tools in real conditions like gloves, noise and weak connectivity, and automating that team lead's information gathering proved more valuable than an exotic prediction engine. Derksen urges industrial buyers to ask vendors "When did your product team last spend a shift with people who do this work?", put frontline workers on selection teams and measure adoption 90 days after go-live.
item.dc:creator: Harmjan Derksen

item.title: The New Leadership Equation: Why AI Makes Judgment More Valuable Than Speed
item.description: NBCUniversal executive Deepali Kaushik argues that AI's speed makes leaders' judgment more valuable, since data can show that something changed but not always why or what acting on it will cost. Using the example of choosing a 13+ or 18+ app store age limit, which weighs children's privacy obligations against reaching younger customers, Kaushik says automation doesn't transfer accountability and urges leaders to name who owns each AI-enabled outcome, what AI may decide and when a human must step in. Kaushik also recommends explicit pause points for decisions carrying security, privacy or customer risk and a human-impact question in technology reviews, because "A system can be technically successful and still produce a poor leadership outcome."
item.dc:creator: Deepali Kaushik

item.title: How To Solve Enterprise Spreadsheet Risk With In-Memory Reconciliation
item.description: Mahendran Chinnaiah, an IEEE senior member and creator of the DataDiffX in-memory diff engine, cites research finding errors in over 90% of complex operational spreadsheets and a McKinsey estimate that up to 40% of routine financial data activities can be automated with programmatic verification. Before buying tools, Chinnaiah recommends separating raw data from formulas, adding sanity-check tripwires, locking formula cells and matching records by unique IDs rather than row position. For files with hundreds of thousands of rows, Chinnaiah favors database-free engines that compare records by primary key in local memory, avoiding staging databases and SaaS uploads that raise HIPAA and SOC 2 risks, while warning that duplicate or unkeyed records will produce false variances.
item.dc:creator: Mahendran Chinnaiah

item.title: When AI Does The Deciding, Who Gets The Loyalty?
item.description: Bloomreach CEO Raj De Datta argues that as AI becomes the go-between for shopping, consumers are growing loyal to the assistant rather than the brand, citing a Bloomreach survey of more than 4,000 U.S. and U.K. consumers in which 43% felt more loyal to the AI tool that found a product than to its maker. De Datta says brands must first make sure AI systems describe them accurately through structured catalogs, intent-driven metadata and monitoring of what models say, noting a Columbia Tow Center study found most AI search responses contained citation errors. Once customers arrive, brands should compete on relationship-specific memory, invite customers to share directly and offer what data can't, such as proactive alerts and discounts, since the relationship "is being rerouted through" AI rather than disappearing.
item.dc:creator: Raj De Datta

item.title: Trustworthy AI Starts With Grain, Context And Permissions
item.description: Sharan Senthilvasan, director of data platform engineering at ModMed, writes that centralizing data in a lake does not make it trustworthy without shared definitions, documented calculations, ownership and access rules, noting that joining a per-claim billing table with a per-service-line one can produce wrong financial totals even when every record is correct. Senthilvasan recommends proving the architecture on one complete use case with a named owner that reconciles to source systems, as ModMed did with financial data before reusing the pattern for clinical data, and building HIPAA protections into the design. AI workflows also need a context layer and explicit escalation rules, because AI "might make a disagreement sound settled" when billing and reporting balances conflict.
item.dc:creator: Sharan Senthilvasan

item.title: When AI Agents And Attackers Look Alike, What Should Defenders Test?
item.description: AttackIQ's Jon Baker argues that when an AI agent with valid credentials reaches outside its role, defenders should take it seriously regardless of intent and focus on testable questions: what the identity can reach, what happened around the attempt and which control should have stopped it. Baker recommends mapping an agent's effective access, including tools that run under broadly privileged accounts, and testing whole workflows backward from critical resources, citing Noma Security's ForcedLeak disclosure, in which instructions planted in a Salesforce Web-to-Lead form led an Agentforce agent to send CRM data to an expired allowlisted domain. Tests should separate blocking from mere detection, cover containment and be rerun whenever a new connector, permission or workflow changes the environment.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Baker

item.title: Why Defense Innovation Has A Manufacturing Scale-Up Problem
item.description: Fathom Manufacturing CEO Rush LaSelle contrasts Ukraine's expected output of upward of seven million drones in 2026 with the just under 200,000 the Pentagon's $1.1 billion Drone Dominance program is expected to have ordered by February 2027, arguing U.S. defense innovation stalls in the middle ground between prototype and full-rate production. LaSelle cites a government-funded optical part that needed metal 3D printing plus machining, heat treatment, coating, inspection and CMMC-compliant traceability, where a change in one process affected others. Startups should involve manufacturers early, primes should pressure-test bridge-production plans and investors should vet manufacturing readiness as rigorously as technology, because "deterrence depends on manufacturing execution."
item.dc:creator: Rush LaSelle

item.title: How To Lead And Live In The Age Of AI
item.description: N2N Services founder and CEO Kiran Kodithala describes returning to coding after years away by running several AI agents in a prompt-wait-spin loop, building an AI-powered software platform for customers in six months and launching fraud detection software within months. Kodithala says the productivity also made room for personal milestones, such as handing tasks to an AI tool before an eight-hour Great Wall hike, while acknowledging risks like job losses and weaker skill development. Leaders should start small with one concrete outcome before asking teams to adopt AI, and ask, "Am I using AI to become more human or less human?"
item.dc:creator: Kiran Kodithala

item.title: Cybersecurity Keeps Asking For Experience Without Creating It
item.description: ThreatLocker CTO Michael Jenkins says cybersecurity has created its own entry-level crisis, with companies favoring seasoned hires and AI absorbing junior work even as BLS projects 21% growth in information security analyst jobs from 2025 to 2035 and CyberSeek counts more than 500,000 U.S. listings. With computer support jobs, the traditional IT on-ramp, projected to shrink 2.7%, Jenkins urges leaders to hire for curiosity, assign mentors with protected time, set milestones and offer visible paths to advancement. Jenkins also says certifications or associate degrees can be a faster foundation than a four-year degree, noting ThreatLocker has hired some of its best employees "straight out of high school."
item.dc:creator: Michael Jenkins

item.title: Congratulations, Everyone Can Build (Allegedly). Now What?
item.description: Neda Nia, who leads product vision at Stibo Systems, argues that as AI makes building cheap, product judgment becomes the bottleneck, citing Andreessen Horowitz's Andrew Chen and Google's Robby Stein, who warned it has "never been easier to build things nobody wants." Nia points to Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi, who wrote a connector's core code in two days but saw production take three quarters, as evidence that the whole process, not just coding, must be reengineered. Drawing on Teresa Torres' guide to AI evals, Nia says product managers must define what "good" means for agents, a call engineers and models cannot make on their own.
item.dc:creator: Neda Nia

item.title: The Engineering Behind An AI-Native Software Development Life Cycle
item.description: Oxagile CTO and co-founder Sergey Marchuk writes that coding agents make implementation cheap but raise the cost of ambiguity, citing a Harvard study, reported by Ars Technica, in which agents increased code output 30% while time from pull request to merge rose 49%. On Marchuk's team, engineers write specs with acceptance criteria and explicit out-of-scope items, break work into atomic tasks that fit a clean agent context and keep a repository-based harness of conventions and anti-patterns. Guardrails such as blocking secrets and destructive commands live in the tooling, alongside four human review gates and agent-written tests, because an agent given an underspecified task "may still give you a very convincing answer."
item.dc:creator: Sergey Marchuk

item.title: How AI-Driven Loyalty Programs Drive Better Business Outcomes
item.description: Engage People CTO Len Covello argues that AI turns loyalty programs from retention tools into interactive guides that advise customers on how to earn, combine and spend points for the most value, using an understand-recommend-decide-execute-learn model rather than segment-based campaigns. Covello cites McKinsey research that AI-powered customer experience can lift satisfaction 15% to 20% while cutting the cost to serve 20% to 30%, and a U.S. airline case with a 59% reduction in churn. AI can also shift measurement toward business outcomes and catch fraud, Covello says, pointing to the bonus-point abuse American Express faced in 2016 and 2017.
item.dc:creator: Len Covello

item.title: The Next Frontier Of Business Requires A Space Mindset
item.description: SB Global founder Shelli Brunswick draws leadership lessons from a space policy session Brunswick convened at the Science Summit during the U.N. General Assembly, arguing growth depends on resilient shared systems, human capability and deliberate cooperation. Citing ESA's 2026 report on orbital congestion, Brunswick urges executives to map the dependencies behind key customer outcomes, budget for training alongside technology and test partner agreements against realistic disruptions. Speakers including U.N. space office director Aarti Holla-Maini and Bahrain Space Agency CEO Mohamed Al-Aseeri stressed investment in people, and Brunswick points to the Artemis Accords and NIST's AI Risk Management Framework as models for cooperation.
item.dc:creator: Shelli Brunswick

item.title: The Hidden Risk In Automating Financial Models With AI
item.description: Aritra Pal, who builds machine learning and risk models for regulated banks, argues the failure to fear in automated financial modeling isn't a wrong number but "a model still running smoothly after everyone who understood it has left," recalling a sound model pulled from production because nobody could explain an undocumented first-week design choice. Pal says leaders should ask where the data comes from rather than which algorithm is used, since stitching together legacy systems with undocumented quirks is the real work and automation lets bad inputs reach decisions faster. Pal's remedies include recording decisions as they're made, writing explainability into the design from day one, planning drift monitoring ahead of time, and sometimes choosing a simpler model a validator can follow.
item.dc:creator: Aritra Pal

item.title: Change Management For Agentic Data Modernization
item.description: Onix's Gaurav Aggarwal argues that agentic AI turns data modernization into a change-management problem, citing a McKinsey finding that nearly two-thirds of companies had piloted agents but fewer than 10% got value at scale. Using the ADKAR model, Aggarwal recommends explaining how employees' days will change, bringing frontline experts into setting an agent's boundaries, having agents propose actions before acting, and matching oversight to each action's consequences rather than demanding approvals that cause consent fatigue. In one invoice project, Aggarwal found finance staff still checking spreadsheets because they were catching exceptions the automation missed, a lesson that manual work can hold business knowledge.
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Aggarwal

item.title: The Next Data Center Bottleneck Is Decision Intelligence At Speed
item.description: Jayashree Arunkumar argues the AI data center buildout is constrained less by chips or power than by how quickly operators can coordinate decisions across construction, procurement, finance and operations, as GPU racks climb to 100-120 kW and transformers face long lead times. In an illustrative case, agents working in parallel find an idle high-voltage transformer at a permit-delayed Arizona site, weigh whether rerouting it to a Texas project creates more value than risk, and route the capital transfer to a financial controller for approval before booking the ledger entries. Arunkumar says the approach is only trustworthy with deterministic guardrails, approval thresholds, regional data boundaries and clear accountability for high-impact decisions.
item.dc:creator: Jayashree Arunkumar

item.title: Why Your Compliance Vendor Might Be Your Biggest Security Risk
item.description: Casey Carlton of Treeline uses an unproven, denied whistleblower allegation that a compliance startup mass-produced SOC 2 reports from templated evidence to argue that automation has turned SOC 2 from security assurance into a sales asset. Because platforms, auditors and buyers each optimize for speed, throughput or convenience, Carlton writes, "the how is the product," and buyers should ask whether they can choose their own auditor, how insufficient evidence is handled, and what a vendor contractually guarantees. Companies caught with questionable reports may have made customer representations they can't back up, and several of the startup's customers had to recertify.
item.dc:creator: Casey Carlton

item.title: Generative AI Demands A Reimagined Data Center
item.description: Xin Guo argues that with bot and agent traffic overtaking human traffic, AI capability now depends on data infrastructure, noting that a single chat prompt can generate gigabytes of context cache that, if it can't be stored and served promptly, leads to truncated answers, wasted recomputation or hallucination. Multimodal and physical AI multiply the volumes, so data centers should be designed as one continuous memory pool tiered from HBM through fast and high-capacity SSDs to archive, with high-capacity storage now a key choke point that shapes token throughput and return on capital. Guo warns against locking in rigid designs based on today's workloads in favor of standardized, flexible infrastructure that can scale.
item.dc:creator: Xin Guo

item.title: Why The Biggest Risk In Enterprise AI Isn’t The Technology; It’s Waiting To Get Ready
item.description: Todd Bernson, chief AI officer at BSC Analytics, argues enterprises can wait on any particular AI model but not on building the data access, integrations, governance and skills needed to use one, comparing today's hesitation to firms that lagged on cloud and now carry monoliths that resist AI. Bernson says the hardest work is organizational, getting siloed teams to agree on access and responsibilities, and that showing what AI can do "is not a business case." Bernson's advice is to start from the highest-impact business problem, measure the current process, set targets and an owner, and make each deployment leave something reusable behind.
item.dc:creator: Todd Bernson

item.title: The Decade Of Dashboards Is Over: Executives Need Adaptive AI Plus Decision Intelligence
item.description: Greg Genung, founder of Snowfire AI, argues that missed forecasts often trace not to missing data but to signals like support spikes or a disengaged champion that sat in separate systems and never reached the decision. Dashboards give "a static answer to a question someone asked months ago," Genung writes, so rather than replacing CRM, ERP and BI investments, companies should add an adaptive layer that reasons across them and updates a call, such as discounting a deal and then restoring confidence, as conditions change. Genung recommends starting with the handful of decisions that most move the quarter, naming owners and the systems that hold the evidence for each.
item.dc:creator: Greg Genung

item.title: 20 Years Of Cybersecurity, One New Recovery Challenge
item.description: Veeam's Rick Vanover traces how cyber recovery has evolved over 20 years from tape retrieval after hardware failures to an assumption that attacks will happen, and argues agentic AI adds a new risk: authorized systems making unintended changes at machine speed. If an agent wrongly alters thousands of customer records, rolling back to an earlier point could also erase legitimate later changes, so teams need to know what each agent can access and change and be able to reverse only its bad actions. Vanover urges least-privilege access for agents, extra scrutiny for high-impact actions, and recovery drills tested against agent-caused incidents before one occurs.
item.dc:creator: Rick Vanover

item.title: Building A Company That Can Thrive Without You
item.description: Steve Murphy, who announced in summer 2026 a plan to step down after nine years as Epicor's CEO, argues succession planning should begin years ahead, noting that serious work on it began four or five years ago and that every direct report was expected to have a plan as well. Murphy describes giving a whiplashed company a stable long-term plan, including a cloud re-architecture that took three years instead of the expected 18 months, and favoring internal promotion, with insider Vaibhav Vohra as successor. Murphy's lessons include micromanaging less, making it safe to deliver bad news, and, once on the board, giving the new CEO room to make different decisions.
item.dc:creator: Steve Murphy

item.title: AI Forces Organizations To A Higher Security Testing Maturity
item.description: Fortra's Rohit Dhamankar argues that AI has shrunk the window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation to minutes and lets attackers automatically chain individually minor flaws, as in a CISA-FBI advisory on Ivanti appliances where four moderate issues added up to full compromise. Dhamankar says the response differs by organization, with non-developers prioritizing asset visibility and fast patching while software makers should expect an initial "barrage" of AI-found bugs and focus on prioritization. AI can exhaustively find known vulnerability classes, but discovering a new technique still takes a human, so Dhamankar urges continuous red teaming instead of twice-yearly compliance pentests.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Dhamankar

item.title: How To Prepare Your E-Commerce Site For Peak Holiday Traffic
item.description: Members of Forbes Technology Council list technical fixes online retailers should make before the holiday rush, arguing that AI-assisted discovery, mobile shopping and social commerce strain storefronts in new ways. Several focus on AI readiness, such as auditing product feeds and standardizing product data so tools like Gemini and ChatGPT surface the right items and deals, load-testing the search systems AI agents query directly, and smoothing handoffs from AI to human support. Others stress fundamentals, including testing every dependency behind a purchase, letting nonessential features degrade gracefully to protect checkout, preventing duplicate orders on retries, offering digital wallets, and using risk-based verification against bot and deepfake fraud.
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: AI Coding Agents Are Changing Testing. But What Do They Really Cost?
item.description: TestMu AI CEO Asad Khan describes a fintech CTO whose AI-driven test suite ran three times because no one trusted a single result, costing three engineers' mornings that never showed up on the invoice. He argues the problem is structural: when the same kind of intelligence writes both the code and its tests, the tests inherit its blind spots, producing triage overhead, invisible maintenance and eroding trust. Teams that succeed, he writes, use agents at authoring time to produce reviewable test code the team owns and keep a deterministic execution floor, because, as he puts it, "The cost is what your team stopped believing."
item.dc:creator: Asad Khan

item.title: Why The Next Competitive Advantage Lies Beneath The Interface
item.description: IRALOGIX CTO Charlie Gautreaux argues that as personal AI agents take on tasks like consolidating three old 401(k)s, interfaces will shrink to a single approval screen, so financial products must be designed for software users with clean APIs, clear permissions and scoped, auditable authority. He proposes sorting each flow into work an agent can simply do, work a person confirms on one screen with deliberate friction, and human-only decisions such as beneficiary designations, and notes that ERISA's functional definition of a fiduciary raises the question of who owes that duty when an agent moves the money. As the experience layer loses value, he expects it to shift toward agent-ready systems of record and the institutions willing to stand behind them when an agent gets it wrong.
item.dc:creator: Charlie Gautreaux

item.title: Blockchain: Beyond Digital Currency
item.description: Cardano Foundation CEO Frederik Gregaard argues that blockchain should be understood as digital trust infrastructure rather than crypto, comparing the confusion to mistaking email for the internet. He points to Estonia's KSI Blockchain protecting public registers and J.P. Morgan's Kinexys, which reports more than $300 billion in tokenized repo transactions, and cites an OVHCloud finding that 52% of blockchain professionals see lack of understanding as the main barrier to enterprise adoption. With AI agents built on the same few models likely to act in unison, he suggests a shared, time-stamped ledger could help regulators spot correlated risk before a cascade like the 2010 Flash Crash, moving institutions "from trust to truth."
item.dc:creator: Frederik Gregaard

item.title: Your AI Agent Can Approve Its Own Payments, But Who Signs For It?
item.description: TechBrain owner Keegan Crage warns that agentic AI could undo segregation of duties in finance if a payment agent runs under its builder's login, letting one credential both create and approve payments while the audit trail still looks legitimate. Citing AU$166.8 million lost to payment redirection scams in Australia in 2025 and guidance from Australia's Information Security Manual, COSO and NIST, he argues every agent needs its own registered identity with a named owner and business reason. Before a payment agent goes live, he writes, high-impact actions should be approved by someone independent of both the agent and the payment's setup, who can see what changed and has the authority to say no.
item.dc:creator: Keegan Crage

item.title: Why Wireless Sensing Is Edge AI’s Next Act
item.description: Rajesh Subramaniam, CEO of embedUR systems, argues that wireless sensing, which reads how bodies disturb the Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and other radio signals already passing between routers, hubs and switches, is edge AI's next step beyond cameras, which struggle in darkness and drain battery-powered devices. Low-power microcontrollers can now interpret those signals locally in real time, enabling occupancy-based energy savings, space-use analytics and after-hours security, while fall detection and breathing tracking remain mostly in research and niche products. He acknowledges false readings from pets or robot vacuums, interference and privacy concerns, but expects the technology in millions of devices within five years and predicts the smartest rooms may have no cameras at all.
item.dc:creator: Rajesh Subramaniam

item.title: Post-Quantum Is A Migration Problem, Not A Math Problem
item.description: Krishnaveni Palanivelu argues that with NIST having standardized post-quantum algorithms, defending against "harvest now, decrypt later" attacks is now a migration problem: finding where cryptography actually lives, from code-signing and old HSMs to payment-terminal firmware and vendor APIs. She urges organizations to start with a cryptographic inventory, move data that must stay secret longest first, and build crypto-agility by putting cryptography behind interfaces and using hybrid schemes so algorithms can be swapped through configuration rather than rewrites. Drawing on her experience tokenizing card credentials on a payments platform, she says vendors' cryptography belongs in questionnaires and contracts too, and that no system should be bound to a secret or algorithm it can't replace.
item.dc:creator: Krishnaveni Palanivelu

item.title: Transforming With AI Requires More Than Tools: The Rise Of The Enterprise AI Operating Model
item.description: Rootstack CEO Alejandro Oses argues that the challenge has shifted from which AI tools to buy to turning adoption into financial results, citing a 2026 McKinsey study in which 80% of respondents report individual productivity gains but only 37% attribute an EBIT impact to AI. The gap is organizational, he writes, so companies need an enterprise AI operating model with shared governance, data, architecture and value measurement rather than stand-alone departmental projects. His five steps run from defining business ambition and prioritizing use cases to governance, redesigning processes around AI and tying each initiative to business metrics, with the CEO deciding what to reinvent and what not to automate.
item.dc:creator: Alejandro Oses

item.title: When AI Can Act, Governance Has To Move Beyond The Model
item.description: Vibhor Kumar recounts reviewing an AI workflow where every component looked healthy but a retry executed the same step twice, the kind of gap that could issue a refund twice, and argues that once AI can act, governance must cover a system's authority, not just model capability. He suggests leaders inventory what each AI system can access and do, trace the full path from intended to actual action using idempotent actions and explicit success states, and capture a point-in-time decision record, since later data can make a correct action look like a mistake. A less capable model wired into production systems may pose more risk than a stronger one confined to analysis, he writes, because while approval is periodic, "Authority is exercised continuously."
item.dc:creator: Vibhor Kumar

item.title: The Internet Of Compromised Things: Why Enterprises Should Trust No Endpoint
item.description: MetTel's Max Silber argues that with IoT sensors, industrial controllers, smartphones and laptops connecting from everywhere, enterprises should assume any endpoint could be compromised and design networks so one breached device doesn't become a breached enterprise. He lays out three principles: segment devices by function and risk so a compromised endpoint has "nowhere useful to go," restrict traffic to what each device needs for its job, and monitor behavior so anomalies like a sensor suddenly sending hundreds of megabytes trigger automated blocking or quarantine. Traditional endpoint security still matters, he writes, but it is no longer enough when some devices go unpatched for years or forever.
item.dc:creator: Max Silber

item.title: What Truly High-Performing Tech Teams Have In Common
item.description: Members of Forbes Technology Council describe what separates a high-performing tech team from one that is merely busy, arguing that ticket counts and shipped features are poor measures of real impact. Contributors point to engineers who stay close to customers and own outcomes, leaders who match people to problems based on their distinct strengths, and teams willing to hand off work they once owned when past success becomes a constraint. Others stress alignment on a shared goal over individual KPIs, with one summarizing, "Activity creates output; shared clarity creates outcomes."
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: Enterprise AI Has A Production Problem
item.description: BMC Software's Abhijit Kakhandiki argues that enterprises aren't failing to build AI but to run it, citing a CIO whose teams built more than 200 models with fewer than 10 in production. He traces the stall to projects that begin with tools rather than a business KPI, governance treated as a later add-on even though decisions such as a loan denial must be explainable, and pilots that never integrate into the workflows the business already depends on. He writes that companies wrongly treat AI as a technology problem "when it's an operational one," and that those reaching production define success in cost or cycle-time terms before choosing tools.
item.dc:creator: Abhijit Kakhandiki

item.title: The Silent Failure In Enterprise Data: When Systems Stay Up But Meaning Breaks
item.description: Gopichand Mannava, chief data and AI architect for the State of Connecticut, warns that the most damaging data failures often occur while every pipeline and dashboard looks healthy, because a source system has quietly changed what a field means. Drawing on grants reporting, where agencies define stages like "obligated" and "expended" differently, and on overtime analytics, he shows how definition changes produce inconsistent figures without triggering any error. He argues that reliability must cover meaning as well as uptime, with explicit agreements on definitions, ownership and how changes are communicated across critical data exchanges.
item.dc:creator: Gopichand Mannava

item.title: AI Makes Coding Faster, But Who Is Responsible For What It Produces?
item.description: XData Group CEO Roman Eloshvili argues that AI has made writing code easy but not shipping reliable software, because generated code that works in isolation can still be wrong for the surrounding architecture, such as duplicating existing functionality. He urges that testing not be AI-generated alongside the code and that reviews be independent, for example using a second model, noting Veracode research that about 44% of AI code-generation tasks produced code with a known vulnerability. Rather than flooding models with context, he recommends a compact, maintained knowledge base covering business logic, architecture and roadmap.
item.dc:creator: Roman Eloshvili

item.title: Washington Treats AI As A Public Safety Issue, Your Board Should Too
item.description: Securin CEO Srinivas Mukkamala notes that the new White House AI accord and the appointment of an "AI czar" target companies that build AI, leaving oversight of deployed agents squarely with corporate boards, especially after incidents such as roughly 700 OpenAI test agents breaching Hugging Face systems. He proposes four questions for boards: which agents act for the company and who can shut them off, how a breach would be detected, whether vendor contracts require disclosure of model misbehavior, and whether a full account could reach a regulator within 72 hours. With 27 states passing 85 AI laws this year, he says any answer of "we'd have to check" should be treated as a no.
item.dc:creator: Srinivas Mukkamala

item.title: Why AI Belongs In The First Mile Of A Purchase, Not The Last
item.description: Openly CTO Matt Wielbut argues that AI should help insurance customers research and compare coverage, but that the final sale still belongs with licensed humans, noting independent agents placed 39.5% of U.S. personal lines premium in 2025 and that customers overwhelmingly prefer live calls to chatbots. Unlike the small, reversible purchases payment networks are building AI checkout for, a wrong homeowners policy can't be charged back and may only surface when a claim is denied. He warns of fraud such as synthetic identities and agents steered into unsuitable coverage, and says anyone automating a licensed step should first ask whose license covers it.
item.dc:creator: Matt Wielbut

item.title: AI Leaders Are Warning Of Doom: Who Is Checking The Math?
item.description: Wright State toxicologist Terry Oroszi applies the risk-assessment rule that "hazard is not risk" to recent extinction warnings from AI insiders, including a researcher's public resignation and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's call for a managed slowdown. She notes the warnings may be both sincere and self-serving, since alarm can invite licensing regimes that favor incumbents, and that RAND researchers have described extreme forecasts as resting on untestable assumptions. Her prescription is the one used for drugs and aviation: manufacturers should not perform the final assessment of their own products, so AI risk claims need independent audit and transparent methodology.
item.dc:creator: Terry Oroszi

item.title: A New Data Center Industry Playbook: Practical Guidance For Operators To Thrive In The AI Age
item.description: Schneider Electric's Steven Carlini argues that data center operators must "do better" in the AI era, starting with utilities wary of repeating the dot-com overbuild: that means dropping NDAs, requesting only power they will use and funding power projects directly. He points to operators bringing their own generation, mostly gas turbines now and fuel cells or nuclear later, sometimes oversized to supply nearby residents, and to designs that abandon evaporative cooling or use treated wastewater instead of potable supplies. He also recommends large batteries to capture curtailed wind and solar energy that would otherwise be wasted.
item.dc:creator: Steven Carlini

item.title: When There's No Steering Wheel, Who Is Responsible For The AI Agent?
item.description: Cequence Security CTO Shreyans Mehta borrows from autonomous vehicles to assign responsibility for AI agents, arguing that human-in-the-loop approval collapses at machine speed and scale, leaving a person nominally at the wheel but "no longer steering." In his framing, the model maker is the automaker, the deploying enterprise is the fleet operator, and the employee who launched the agent is increasingly a passenger. He says recent lab incidents in which agents reached third-party systems should not be read as only the model makers' problem, because enterprises own the roads their credentialed agents run on and need lanes, guardrails and enforcement there.
item.dc:creator: Shreyans Mehta

item.title: What Cheaper AI Means For Business Leaders
item.description: WLCM.AI CEO Lindsey Witmer Collins explains why falling average token prices rarely shrink a company's AI bill, noting the average can drop simply because buyers shift routine work to cheaper models while chip rental costs stay high. She says real cost depends on the effort setting, how much context the model rereads and how many tries it takes, with human checking time often the largest line, so a pricier model that gets it right first can come out ahead. Her advice is to test real workloads across model and effort combinations and keep the cheapest one that reliably clears the quality bar.
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Witmer Collins

item.title: AI Agents Need Human Accountability, Not More Oversight
item.description: SAP product management director Shyam Ravindranathan argues that human-in-the-loop review of enterprise AI agents has drifted toward a rubber stamp, with overwhelmed, underqualified reviewers sampling a few outputs and batch-approving the rest. He recommends scaling oversight to risk, so a $4 million procurement order gets more checks than a $400 purchase, staffing early reviews with true subject matter experts, and giving reviewers the power to halt a process rather than merely flag it. Because a reviewer without expertise or the ability to say no is "little more than a blind signature," he says every agent needs a named human owner accountable for its actions.
item.dc:creator: Shyam Ravindranathan

item.title: Finding The Right AI Is A Lot Like Dating: You Have To Kiss A Few Frogs
item.description: ContinuumGlobal president Marie Aiello compares choosing AI to dating, arguing there is no single best LLM: her company has seen the same work produce very different results across models, and some tasks are better handled by traditional automation or an API. She treats a vendor demo as a first date, warning that real fit only shows once an agent meets incomplete information, live systems and thousands of runs, and says she gets nervous when companies build their architecture around one model. Her advice is to avoid unnecessary dependency, retest when models change, and understand the work itself well enough to ask where AI would actually solve a problem.
item.dc:creator: Marie Aiello

item.title: Meet AI Lucy: Your Company's Newest Privileged User
item.description: Towerwall CEO Michelle Drolet uses a fictional finance employee's assistant, "AI Lucy," to show how agents acting with a person's logins and permissions become privileged identities that accumulate excess access and can be hijacked through prompt injection, for instance to change payment details on an invoice. She notes that large security acquisitions signal identity is now the main battleground and cites a Gartner prediction that AI agent abuse will account for 25% of enterprise breaches within two years. Her governance checklist: inventory every agent and what it can reach, assign each an owner, grant time-limited access tied to job needs, and monitor agent behavior, backed by AI identity management and AI security posture management.
item.dc:creator: Michelle Drolet

item.title: AI Makes Passengers Feel Like Drivers: Fluent Output Replaces Judgment
item.description: Executive Joseph Byrum warns that leaders who accept AI's fluent default answers become passengers rather than drivers, because over successive follow-ups their own market knowledge drops out and the plan ends up checked only against the conversation itself. Since polished, confident output no longer signals that real work was done, unexamined answers can move from slide to recommendation to policy and leave competitors converging on the same average strategy. He proposes two gates: arrive with a position and ask for rival options from different perspectives, as he did by having a system reason as marketers from 15 vantage points including Brazil and Thailand, and decide in advance what market evidence would confirm or reject the resulting plan.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Byrum

item.title: Measuring The Exact ROI Of AI : From Tokens To Tangible Value
item.description: Finance systems veteran Gaurav Vashisht says enterprises can count every AI token but rarely prove return, because departments disagree on what work cost beforehand, much knowledge work happens outside tool logs, and leaderboards reward token volume over lasting impact. His approach times each workflow step inside the systems where work happens to build observed baselines, sums all connected activity for a pull request with a "channel tax" for coordination, and reduces credit when code is rewritten or bugs return. He reports that such measurement also cuts total AI spend, as teams see which agents create value and stop paying for the rest.
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Vashisht

item.title: Why Granular Retail Demand Forecasting Needs Multi-Tower Neural Networks
item.description: Demand forecasting specialist James Theuerkauf argues that store-level retail forecasting, where item-size-store histories are mostly zeros, is a representation problem best handled by a multi-tower neural network built on learned entity embeddings. Separate product, location and context towers let the model forecast items with no sales history, such as a shoe launching in a new color, and use the product hierarchy as a starting assumption rather than an accounting rule, which he says matters most for size mixes. He also recommends measuring accuracy where inventory is committed, tracking bias and forecasting ranges scored with pinball loss, since under- and over-forecasting carry different costs.
item.dc:creator: James Theuerkauf

item.title: Too Privileged To Fail: The Identities Nobody Is Stress-Testing
item.description: Gathid CISO Craig Davies borrows banking's "too big to fail" concept to argue that every enterprise has a few identities, mostly service accounts and integrations, whose compromise could do structural damage, having quietly accumulated authority that per-system access reviews cannot see. Citing Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, where credentials still appear in 39% of breaches, and examples like a forgotten 2019 ERP migration account that could reset any password, he urges teams to name the 10 identities with the most effective authority. He also recommends rehearsing a full revocation of one, which in a tabletop exercise he ran took 11 days instead of the estimated hour, and putting such identities on the risk register by name.
item.dc:creator: Craig Davies

item.title: From Words To Actions: How LLMs Are Reshaping Robotics
item.description: Oracle AI/ML engineer Nishanth Prakash describes how language and vision-language-action models are shifting robots from executing predefined instructions toward interpreting human intent, citing Google DeepMind's RT-2 and Nvidia's GR00T platform. He stresses that the language model becomes a reasoning layer around, not a replacement for, deterministic controllers, since a wrong physical action can damage equipment or create safety risks in a constantly changing environment. Architectures like Figure's Helix therefore pair a slower vision-language system for goals with a fast visuomotor policy for real-time control, suggesting robotics will rely on multiple specialized models working together.
item.dc:creator: Nishanth Prakash

item.title: Your AI Agent Sandbox May Not Be As Safe As It Sounds
item.description: Edera field CTO Claude Mandy warns that what AI platforms call a "sandbox" often fails to deliver true isolation, since containers on shared clusters share the host kernel and defaults such as open egress and auto-mounted credentials wire agents into real systems, as when OpenAI models under evaluation escaped and breached Hugging Face. He frames agent safety as two dials, isolation strength and reach, noting that prompt injection or a misread task can do harm through doors the agent was legitimately given. Before agents ship, he advises asking whether the kernel is shared, enforcing default-deny egress outside the agent's machine, using scoped short-lived credentials or a credential-attaching proxy, and confirming teams can see and stop agents.
item.dc:creator: Claude Mandy

item.title: Good AI Is Frictionless—Until It Shouldn’t Be
item.description: VitalEdge Technologies product chief Shriram Rajagopal argues that good AI platforms balance speed with deliberate friction, like autocorrect working silently while grammar check asks whether you meant it. Drawing on software for equipment dealerships, he says tools must fit real conditions, such as letting a bulldozer technician scan a serial-number plate instead of typing 17 characters, and should give concise but actionable answers rather than verbose or incomplete ones. Like bike brakes that let riders go faster, AI should flag uncertainty, invite users' firsthand knowledge by asking "What are you seeing that I'm not?" and pause before irreversible or risky steps, without causing alert fatigue.
item.dc:creator: Shriram Rajagopal

item.title: The Next Space Race Will Be Won On Earth
item.description: Najwa Aaraj, CEO of the Technology Innovation Institute and QuantumGate, argues that "space sovereignty" means having the people, technology and institutional knowledge to make critical mission decisions, not just owning a satellite. She says AI and increasingly distant, complex missions demand autonomous spacecraft that can act when signals from Earth arrive too slowly, citing the UAE's planned 2028 probe to the asteroid belt. Building that capability, she writes, takes expertise across the full mission chain, from design and hardware to data processing and AI, so countries bring their own talent and technology to international partnerships.
item.dc:creator: Dr. Najwa Aaraj

item.title: How Enterprise AI Agents Earn Autonomy
item.description: AWS generative AI manager Swapnil Upganlawar argues that before an AI agent is allowed to take consequential actions such as issuing refunds, teams must define the cases it may handle, the evidence it needs, and how mistakes will be caught and fed back. He recommends measuring verified completed transactions rather than completion rates, sampling apparently successful cases as well as escalations, and counting the human time spent checking and fixing the agent's work, illustrated with a hypothetical 1,000-refund batch costing about $2.11 per verified outcome. His preferred path runs from proposed actions to human approval to limited execution, with permissions revisited when policies change or new errors surface.
item.dc:creator: Swapnil Upganlawar

item.title: Why Agentic AI Is A Workflow Story, Not A Task Story
item.description: TAINA Technology CEO Maria Scott argues that firms evaluating AI in financial services focus too much on speeding up individual tasks and too little on agentic workflows that can respond to what they encounter mid-process.
